## The Government Announcement On 10 March 2020, the State Council announced the abandonment of the Ticino 2020 project, which envisaged the implementation of new technologies and public services in the Canton of Ticino. The project had been financed with an amount of CHF 10 million, divided among the Municipalities of the Canton.
## No Refunds for Municipalities Despite requests for compensation from the Municipalities, the government has decided not to provide any reimbursement for the money spent on the project. According to the sources, the government claimed that the responsibility for the failure of the project is to be attributed to both parties.

The Ticino 2020 project was presented in 2015 as a plan to develop the economy of the Canton of Ticino. However, the project has been criticised for the lack of clarity and transparency in the management of the funds.

According to the legal provisions defined by article 356 paragraph 1 of the Code of Obligations (CO), it establishes in common, between the social partners, provisions regarding the stipulation, content and termination of the individual employment relationship. In essence, the CCL is a binding agreement signed on the one hand by trade unions and on the other by employers' associations or individual employers. Its primary function is to set minimum standards that must be respected, often acting as a precursor for future legislative innovations, as happened in the past for various regulations on holidays or rest.

item.title: «Tax on health contrary to the agreements»: the Hinny report is now public
item.description: Pascal Hinny's expert opinion on the border agreement: the Italian health tax is an income tax and violates international agreements
item.content:encoded:
The opinion commissioned by Ticino to the professor of tax law of the University of Freiburg has been published in full. The conclusion: the Italian levy is an income tax and violates the Borderers Agreement
The appraisal can now be consulted in full. And it puts black and white the legal reasons on which Ticino based its opposition to the Italian "health tax" on old border workers. It was signed by Pascal Hinny, full professor of tax law at the University of Freiburg, who was instructed by the cantonal tax administration to verify the compatibility of the new levy with the Agreement on frontier workers and with the Convention against double taxation between Switzerland and Italy. The professor's answer is clear: from the Swiss point of view, the tax is a tax and its collection by Italy violates international agreements. The knot is the right of taxation on so-called old frontiersmen. For those who fall under the transitional regime provided for by the Agreement, the income from employee work produced in Switzerland can be taxed exclusively by the Confederation. Until 2033, the border cantons pay 40% of the tax at source to Italy, but this does not change the distribution of tax power: on those incomes Italy cannot apply further taxation. It is precisely on this point that the health tax is applied. The contribution provided by Italy also concerns old border workers who have opted for the Italian health system and is calculated on the net income earned working in Switzerland. The rate is progressive, from 3 to 6%, with a minimum of 30 and a maximum of 200 euros per month. The central part of the appraisal is dedicated precisely to the nature of the withdrawal. Hinny excludes that it can be considered the consideration of a health service. Paying the tax does not in fact entitle you to new coverage, does not extend existing coverage, and failure to pay does not result in loss of health care.

Therefore, an individual consideration directly linked to the payment is missing: an element that distinguishes a causal tax from a tax. According to Hinny, the levy has the typical characteristics of the tax: it is commensurate with the income from work produced in Switzerland, is progressive and finances public purposes without attributing a specific benefit to the individual taxpayer in return. The resources can also be used for purposes other than individual health coverage. Hence the conclusion. The health tax is, both according to Swiss law and according to the interpretation of the Convention, a tax on income from work. And since for old frontier workers that income is reserved for Swiss tax authorities, Italy cannot unilaterally introduce a second levy on the same taxable amount. For Hinny, therefore, the tax is incompatible with the Agreement on frontier workers and with the Italy-Switzerland Convention against double taxation.

The issue of road mobility and the validity of driving documents directly affects workers who daily cross the customs to reach their workplace in the Canton of Ticino. Road traffic regulations specifically govern the position of those who work across the border while maintaining their residence in Italy compared to those who decide to transfer their domicile to Swiss territory. For G permit holders, current provisions generally allow driving with the driving licence issued in the state of origin, provided it is valid and meets international requirements. The administrative situation changes significantly when the worker modifies their residential status, moving from a mere cross-border regime to a stable settlement with a residence permit. Knowing regulatory obligations precisely avoids administrative sanctions and guarantees full regularity during daily commutes along the roads connecting the border provinces with the main Ticino economic centers.
### Regulatory framework for cross-border drivers The provisions applicable to the circulation of vehicles and enabling documents are based on bilateral agreements and cantonal regulations adopted by the federal authorities. Checks carried out at customs crossings regularly verify the compliance of driving documentation in relation to the driver's status. Those who regularly cross the border must pay attention to the expiry dates of their personal documents and driving licence, distinguishing between the requirements applicable to commuter workers and those reserved for those who establish a primary residence in Switzerland. To explore the overall economic impact of cross-border work, including aspects related to travel, it is useful to consult the online [calculator](nav:calculator). The administrative management of the driver's license for those operating in the Swiss labor market requires careful planning of deadlines and knowledge of the requirements demanded by the competent authorities. When a worker crosses the border with a G permit, the Italian driver's license remains valid for driving on Swiss territory in accordance with current regulations. However, if changes occur in the residency status, there is an obligation to proceed with the conversion of the document at the designated cantonal offices. This bureaucratic step involves submitting specific forms, verifying psycho-physical requirements, and, in some cases, complying with strict time limits established by law to avoid the expiration of driving privileges.
### Medical checks and specific requirements A fundamental element of the procedure concerns the health assessments required for certain license categories or upon reaching specific age thresholds set by federal and cantonal provisions. Unlike Italian regulations, the Swiss system provides deadlines and renewal methods that may differ in frequency and the type of medical examinations required. Professional drivers or those holding higher-category licenses must pay particular attention to the directives issued by the cantonal motor vehicle offices.
